question: Can a notwithstanding-clause declaration remain in force indefinitely without renewal?
generated_answer:
In Canada, the notwithstanding clause, also known as Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, allows the federal government or a provincial government to override certain provisions of the Charter for a period of five years. This means that a law or provision that would otherwise be in conflict with the Charter can be protected from challenge for a limited time.

According to Section 33(3) of the Charter, a declaration made under the notwithstanding clause "shall cease to have effect five years after it comes into force, or on such earlier date as may be specified in the declaration."

However, there is a mechanism for renewing a notwithstanding clause declaration. If a government wants to continue to override a Charter provision beyond the initial five-year period, it can re-enact the declaration, which would then remain in force for another five years. This process can be repeated indefinitely, allowing a government to maintain the override in perpetuity, as long as it continues to re-enact the declaration every five years.

So, to answer your question, a notwithstanding clause declaration cannot remain in force indefinitely without renewal. It must be re-enacted every five years to continue to have effect. If a government fails to re-enact the declaration, it will cease to have effect, and the law or provision will once again be subject to challenge under the Charter.
